Article Title: Being underweight with high BP can be a problem too: Study
Article Text:
Being underweight with high BP can be a problem too: Study

While obesity with hypertension is the most widely recognised high-risk category, a recent study has shown that being underweight with elevated blood pressure or hypertension may also be a high-risk sub-group in Asian populations.The study done in Japan and published in Hypertension Research, an open-source journal in the Nature group of journals, showed the combination of being underweight and having elevated blood pressure or hypertension was associated with increased risk of major adverse cardiovascular events like heart attacks and strokes, particularly among women and among adults aged 40 and above. This is significant for India, where one in five men and women in the 15-49 age group is underweight (body mass index below 18.5)."Conventional prevention strategies for obesity with hypertension appropriately emphasise weight control and cardiometabolic risk reduction; however, the same approach may not be sufficient for underweight individuals with elevated BP or hypertension," stated the study, suggesting the need for additional assessment for unintentional weight loss, malnutrition, low muscle mass, frailty, and underlying chronic disease for those who are underweight with hypertension.Potential management strategies may, therefore, include nutritional assessment and support, resistance exercise or muscle-strengthening interventions where appropriate, and individualised BP control that considers frailty, and symptoms like dizziness or fainting when rising from sitting or lying down.The association between being underweight and cardiovascular events and mortality has been observed in previous studies but significance of high blood pressure was not as well studied or understood. This is of particular significance in Asia where being underweight is relatively common and the distribution of BMI is different from Western populations. In India, the latest National Family Health Survey of 2023-24 showed about 20% of men and women above 15 years had elevated blood pressure or were taking medicine to control it.Understanding cardiovascular risk across the full range of BMI, rather than focusing exclusively on obesity, is expected to enhance understanding of risk stratification in hypertension. The study used the nationwise claims and health-check database of Japan for the period Jan 2005 to Oct 2023 and analysed 62.6 lakh adults without prior cardiovascular disease, chronic renal failure, dialysis, or antihypertensive medication use.
Article Summary: Being underweight with elevated blood pressure or hypertension may also be a high-risk sub-group in Asian populations. This is significant for India, where one in five men and women in the 15-49 age group is underweight (body mass index below 18.5)."Conventional prevention strategies for obesity with hypertension appropriately emphasise weight control," says study.

Article Title: 'Bogus movement led by bogus leader': Union minister takes jibe at Rahul over ethanol blending row
Article Text:
Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Union minister Pralhad Joshi on Tuesday stepped up his attack on Congress over ethanol blending in petrol row and accused it of misleading the public over the issue.Talking to reporters, Joshi took a jibe at Lok Sabha leader of opposition Rahul Gandhi and said that Congress is trying to stir up "bogus movement led by a bogus leader."“One must understand that this is all part of an effort to appease—not just the minorities, but also Rahul Gandhi. They keep saying things in his favour. The public understands this,” he said.“At a time when crude oil is so expensive—with a base price of Rs 53 for petrol, while ethanol costs between Rs 57 and Rs 71 if derived from maize—there is simply no commercial logic to their claims. We took this initiative to support our farmers and to help the nation become self-reliant, rather than remaining dependent on imports,” he said.Joshi also said that Congress had attempted to launch a campaign against the government on several issues, including electronic voting machines, infiltrators and Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.“Yet, the Congress party tried to stir up a movement—a bogus movement led by a bogus leader, Rahul Gandhi. They've tried everything: questioning EVMs, advocating for infiltrators, and even attacking Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.The public has rejected all of this; they simply did not accept it,” Joshi said.“Just as you need specialised, high-end equipment to test for blood sugar levels or detect cancer, similar equipment and recognised laboratories are required for testing petrol and diesel,” he added.“And who introduced this concept of using specific equipment and recognised labs? It was these very people—back in 2005, during the UPA's tenure—who issued an SOP and introduced the 'Petrol and Diesel Order',” he further said.This comes after Karnataka minister Rizwan Arshad said that the state government stands by its report that oil companies are blending more than 20 per cent ethanol in petrol, despite the companies' rejection of the claim/During a press conference, Arshad said the Karnataka government had last Friday released a report stating that petrol samples from seven districts were tested, and most showed an Ethanol blend above 20 per cent, going up to 31.2 per cent."This is contrary to the government policy that they will blend only E20 fuel," he said.He said the oil manufacturing companies disputed the findings after the state explained where the samples were tested and what methodology was used, claiming the state was wrong"I want to tell everyone in the country, assure them, that the Government of Karnataka stands by its report and claims that oil marketing companies are blending more than 20 per cent Ethanol in petrol, which will cause serious damage to the engines of vehicles, and it will burden the common man," Arshad said.
Article Summary: Union minister Pralhad Joshi stepped up his attack on Congress over ethanol blending in petrol row and accused it of misleading the public over the issue. Joshi took a jibe at Lok Sabha leader of opposition Rahul Gandhi and said that Congress is trying to stir up "bogus movement led by a bogus leader"

NEW DELHI: India’s choked capital could on Tuesday and Wednesday witness yet another attempt at cloud seeding, with the hope that rains provide some relief to its choking residents. In a joint attempt by Delhi International Airport Ltd (DIAL), Delhi govt and IIT Kanpur, a specialised Beechcraft 200 of Bengaluru-based Kyathi Climate is expected to fly to Delhi by noon Tuesday and try to enhance precipitation over the next two days as when could formation happens.Incidentally, a fresh western disturbance is approaching north India that is likely to bring rains to the plains of northwestern India later this week.Delhi had unsuccessfully tried cloud seeding in October 2025.“The aircraft used that time was one that could fly only to an altitude of 10,000 feet and do cloud seeding. The Beechcraft 200 being used now can go up an altitude of 25,000 feet and the company is a specialised one for this task,” said people in the know.The capital is amongst the most polluted cities in the world with AQI levels soaring.Kyathi Climate website describes the company as one that “is primarily committed to continue advances in the field of weather modification, either it is identifying the potential benefits of cloud seeding or monitoring air quality.”About cloud seeding, it says, “We intend to develop new techniques not only to produce artificial rain, which will guarantee monsoon clouds break into torrential rains.”

400+ MBBS seats find no takers even after special vacancy round

NEW DELHI: As many as 411 MBBS seats remained unallotted even after the Medical Counselling Committee (MCC) conducted a special stray vacancy round, with the high fee structure in private medical colleges potentially being one of the factors behind the seats remaining unfilled. Of the 948 vacant MBBS seats included in the special round's seat matrix, only 537 were allotted, leaving 411 unfilled. These vacancies raise questions about the affordability of medical education, particularly in private colleges where fees can run into lakhs of rupees.High costs may have deterred some NEET-qualified candidates from opting for these seats, although the allotment data does not establish the reasons for individual choices.A health ministry official said last year, only around 60-70 MBBS seats had remained vacant. "SC had directed us to conduct four rounds of counselling, but we conducted a fifth round as well. Despite that, more than 400 seats remain without allotments.""In many institutions, fees that were around at Rs 15 lakh have increased to Rs 25 lakh to Rs 30 lakh. Govt medical college seats and those in reputed private institutions are getting filled. Vacancies are concentrated in some private colleges. These institutions need to review their fees structures and the quality of education and infrastructure they offer. If fees remain this high, increasing the number of seats will serve little purpose as students can't afford them," the official said.
Article Summary: Of 948 vacant MBBS seats, only 537 were allotted, leaving 411 unfilled. High costs may have deterred some NEET-qualified candidates from opting for these seats, although the allotment data does not establish the reasons for individual choices.

Article Title: CPCB explains why official AQI is capped at 500 despite private apps showing higher readings
Article Text:
People stroll amid smog as air quality deteriorates in Delhi

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: The Central Pollution Control Board on Tuesday defended its air quality monitoring methodology, explaining why official AQI readings are capped at 500 even as private monitoring apps reported levels as high as 1,800 in Delhi after Diwali.The clarification came amid questions over the wide disparity between government data and readings displayed by private air quality monitoring platforms.The CPCB said the 500-point ceiling was an intentional feature of the National Air Quality Index (NAQI), consistent with international practices. It explained that readings beyond 500 would not change the health advisory, as all such levels fall under the 'Severe' category."The Air Quality Index (AQI) is a tool for effective communication of air quality status to the people in terms that are easy to understand. AQI is an indicative scale designed to convey the likely health implications of prevailing air quality conditions. The AQI category along with the associated health statement is more significant than the corresponding AQI value within that category," the board said in a statement.The CPCB said the official index uses scientifically validated 24-hour rolling averages to assess sustained exposure to pollutants. Private apps, on the other hand, often capture hourly fluctuations through low-cost sensors, which may show sharp spikes in pollution levels.According to the board, the NAQI has six categories - 'Good', 'Satisfactory', 'Moderately Polluted', 'Poor', 'Very Poor' and 'Severe' - within a scale of 0 to 500. It said an AQI reading of 500 or above indicates broadly similar health risks and therefore does not warrant a separate category."Beyond this level the AQI remains in the 'Severe' category and extrapolation of the index would not alter the assigned health impact category. The capping at 500 is thus a design feature of the index, as has been evolved in 2015 methodology of NAQI in line with the prevailing international practice including US EPA AQI scale," it added.CPCB also said private apps could report higher readings during brief pollution spikes but show lower figures when pollution levels subsequently decline."It is generally perceived that private apps show higher AQI. This may hold during short peaks, when hourly values rise sharply. However, when concentrations fall, such apps show lower AQI than the NAQI, since the NAQI continues to reflect the exposure of the preceding 24 hours," it said."This has also been evident in Delhi post Diwali firecrackers bursting event. The NAQI thus provides a consistent and reliable indication of the likely health impacts of sustained exposure to pollutants, which is the scientifically relevant measure for public health advisories," it further said.The clarification came as social media posts showing screenshots of private air quality apps reporting AQI levels between 1,500 and 1,800 in Delhi on Diwali night, while CPCB's official readings remained below 400.
Article Summary: The Central Pollution Control Board defended its air quality monitoring methodology. It said the 500-point ceiling was an intentional feature of the National Air Quality Index (NAQI) The board said readings beyond 500 would not change the health advisory, as all such levels fall under 'Severe' category.

Article Title: 'Silent on hate crimes against Indians': MEA tears into US agency over religious freedom report

NEW DELHI: What began withhas grown into one of the world's largest vaccination drives. Now, smallpox is history, polio has been eliminated, and maternal and neonatal tetanus are no longer public health threats in India.That's quite a flex!India's vaccination story is one of ambitious campaigns, millions of doses and some remarkable public health victories. The country was declared polio-free in 2014. A year later, it eliminated maternal and neonatal tetanus as a public health problem. Then, during the Covid-19 pandemic, it administered over 200 crore vaccine doses, including indigenously developed and licensed vaccines manufactured in India.And the drive is far from over.Earlier this year, the government added another shot to India's public health armoury with a nationwide human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination campaign for 14-year-old girls, aimed at protecting them against cervical cancer. It also launched an indigenously manufactured tetanus-diphtheria (Td) vaccine. From fighting childhood infections to preventing cancer,India's vaccine drive is continuously levelling up. According to the Union health ministry, full immunisation coverage climbed from 62% in 2015 to 98.4% in January 2026.Last year, the figure stood at 97.9%.However, there is still a long way to go.Lakhs of children are missing essential shots with coverage remaining uneven across states. At the same time, many older adults are still largely missing from the vaccination picture.But if India has come this far, why are so many people still missing their shots?India's vaccination story goes back more than two centuries. The first smallpox vaccination in the country was administered in Mumbai on June 14, 1802, after vaccine lymph arrived from abroad. Nearly a century later, in 1897, Dr Waldemar Haffkine developed India's first indigenous vaccine against plague, also in Bombay.The government's efforts to make immunisation more organised gathered pace in 1962 with the launch of the national BCG programme to control tuberculosis. This was followed by the Expanded Programme on Immunisation (EPI) in 1978, which marked another step towards wider vaccine coverage.However, 1985 proved to be a bigger turning point. India launched the Universal Immunisation Programme (UIP), bringing free vaccines against 12 preventable diseases to children and pregnant women. The initiative laid the foundation for what has since grown into one of the world's largest publicly funded vaccination programmes.The scale of the operation today is enormous. Every year, the UIP reaches 2.9 crore pregnant women and 2.54 crore newborns every year, free of cost . A vast network of government healthcare centres, frontline health workers, cold-chain facilities and digital systems supports the delivery and tracking of these doses.The programme's vaccine basket has also grown over the years. What initially focused on diseases such as tuberculosis, polio and tetanus now offers protection against a wider range of infections, including rotavirus diarrhoea, rubella and serious illnesses caused by pneumococcal bacteria.Alongside this expansion came some major public health victories. India eliminated smallpox, yaws, polio and maternal and neonatal tetanus as public health threats. Immunisation has also contributed to lower child mortality and reduced the burden of diseases such as measles and rubella.One campaign, in particular, became a defining moment in this journey. Launched in 1995, the Pulse Polio Programme took vaccination beyond healthcare centres and turned it into a nationwide public movement. Its now-familiar slogan,, helped bring millions of people into the campaign. The last reported case of wild polio in India was recorded on January 13, 2011, in Howrah, West Bengal. In 2014, the country was certified polio-free.But maintaining high vaccination coverage is an ongoing exercise. Full immunisation coverage stood at 94.7% in 2022-23, slipped to 93.7% in 2023-24, rose to 98.3% in 2024-25 and eased to 97.9% in 2025-26.India has also made progress in reaching children who have not received any routine vaccines, commonly referred to as zero-dose children. Their share declined from 0.11% in 2023 to 0.06% in 2024.Vaccination is not a one-and-done exercise. Some shots are given at birth, others follow at carefully spaced intervals, and a few need boosters to keep protection going. But what exactly do these jabs do?A vaccine essentially prepares the immune system for an encounter with a disease-causing germ. It teaches the body to recognise the threat and respond faster if it comes into contact with it later. This reduces the risk of infection and, in many cases, prevents severe illness.In India, this protection begins at birth. Newborns receive vaccines against tuberculosis (BCG), polio and hepatitis B. The hepatitis B birth dose is particularly time-sensitive and should ideally be administered within the first 24 hours.The next round begins when the baby is six weeks old, with follow-up doses at ten and fourteen weeks. These vaccines protect against diphtheria, whooping cough, tetanus, hepatitis B, polio, rotavirus diarrhoea and infections caused by Haemophilus influenzae type B (Hib).Pneumococcal vaccines are also included in the schedule to protect infants against serious infections, including certain types of pneumonia and meningitis.The vaccination calendar does not stop once babies become toddlers. Between nine and 12 months, children receive their first measles-rubella dose, followed by a second at 16-24 months. Japanese encephalitis vaccines are also offered in endemic districts.As children get older, booster doses become part of the routine. DPT boosters are given during early childhood, followed by tetanus-diphtheria (Td) shots at the ages of ten and 16 to maintain protection.The schedule is also expanding beyond childhood infections, with cancer prevention entering the picture.On February 28, 2026, the government launched a nationwide human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination campaign, offering a free, voluntary, single-dose vaccine to around 1.2 crore girls aged 14. The campaign aims to protect them against HPV infections that can lead to cervical cancer.The rollout has gathered pace, too. By September 11, more than 80 lakh doses had been administered, with Uttar Pradesh accounting for the highest number at over 22 lakh.From a newborn's first vaccines to an adolescent's HPV shot, India's immunisation schedule covers several stages of life. But having vaccines on the calendar is only half the job. Ensuring that every eligible beneficiary receives the right dose at the right time remains the bigger challenge.The latest WHO-UNICEF estimates for 2025 suggest that India is making steady progress in getting more children vaccinated. Around 97% received the first dose of the diphtheria, tetanus and pertussis (DTP) vaccine, while 95% completed all three doses. Measles vaccination coverage was equally encouraging, with 98% of children receiving the first dose and 95% getting the second.There is another milestone worth celebrating. The number of zero-dose children, those who have not received even the first dose of a DTP-containing vaccine, fell from around 9.09 lakh in 2024 to 6.79 lakh in 2025. That's a decline of nearly 25% in just one year.India also achieved a significant first. For the first time since WHO-UNICEF estimates began in 2001, it dropped out of the world's top ten countries with the highest number of children missing measles vaccination.In this case, slipping down the rankings is actually good news!However, the progress is not uniform. WHO's 2025 estimates show that only 70% of newborns received the hepatitis B birth dose within 24 hours, while rotavirus vaccine coverage stood at 91%.India has made steady progress towards universal immunisation, with full vaccination coverage among children aged 12-23 months rising from 83.8% to 87.1%, according to vaccination card records.The household survey also brings out a gap that national averages can easily mask: differences between states. Full vaccination coverage among children aged 12-23 months ranged from 93.8% in Goa to just 64.3% in Nagaland, a gap of nearly 30 percentage points.The divide is visible in hepatitis B vaccination, too. While 91.9% of newborns in Goa received the birth dose, the figure was only 46.4% in Nagaland.In other words, India's vaccination report card may be improving, but the marks are far from evenly distributed. Where a child is born can still make a significant difference to the protection they receive.So, if childhood vaccines are free, why are so many children still missing their shots?The answer lies in barriers that go beyond the availability of vaccines. From caregiver hesitation to migration and poor access to healthcare, several factors can leave children partially or completely unvaccinated.A WHO report from April 2026 offers some insight. Under its TrackVac initiative, the vaccination status of 2,24,698 children was assessed across 143 priority districts in 11 states during 2025. Among children who remained unvaccinated, caregiver refusal accounted for 39% of cases, while migration was responsible for 34%.While these findings are based on targeted districts and do not represent a nationwide survey, they highlight two major hurdles in India's immunisation efforts: vaccine hesitancy and disruptions in access to healthcare.Migration, in particular, can interrupt a child's vaccination schedule. A family moving from one city to another for work may get its baby the first dose but miss subsequent appointments after relocating. In remote villages and underserved urban settlements, long distances, transport costs, limited awareness and the loss of a day's wages can also discourage families from returning for the next dose.Misinformation and fears about side effects add to the challenge. With several vaccines requiring multiple doses, missing even one appointment can leave a child only partially protected.The challenge, therefore, is not just to make vaccines free but also to ensure that families can access them easily, understand their importance and complete the recommended vaccination schedule.For many Indians, the vaccination chapter quietly ends with school, but adults need those shots too!Depending on age, health and vaccination history, adults may benefit from vaccines against influenza, pneumococcal disease, hepatitis B, shingles and other infections.Tetanus-diphtheria boosters still matter, and pregnant women receive tetanus-diphtheria vaccination under India's public immunisation programme. Older adults and people with chronic health conditions face higher risks from certain infections, so age-appropriate vaccination is especially relevant for them.Yet adult vaccination has mostly stayed in the shadows. According to an earlier TOI report, citing older Longitudinal Ageing Study in India data, highlighted strikingly low uptake among older Indians: just 1.59% had received the influenza vaccine, 0.74% the pneumococcal vaccine, 1.82% the hepatitis B vaccine, and 2.75% the tetanus-diphtheria vaccine. These are historical survey figures rather than fresh 2026 measurements, but they show how thin adult coverage has been.India's Covid-19 campaign, which delivered more than 220 crore doses, proved that mass adult immunisation can be done. Yet unlike childhood vaccination, there's still no comparable universal routine programme for older adults.But things are starting to change.In September 2026, Goa became India's first state to adopt a dedicated life-course immunisation policy for 2026-2036, initially focusing on influenza, pneumococcal and hepatitis B vaccines for eligible high-risk adults.Turns out vaccination isn't just a childhood routing but also needs to continue well into adulthood.Finding children who have missed their vaccines is only half the battle. Ensuring they receive every due dose on time remains the bigger challenge.The government has stepped up efforts to close this gap through initiatives such as Mission Indradhanush, which has vaccinated over 5.46 crore children and 1.32 crore pregnant women. The U-WIN portal, which had 11.87 crore children registered as of March 2026, is another step towards better tracking, helping health workers monitor vaccination schedules and send reminders for missed doses.WHO's TrackVac initiative also highlights how targeted follow-ups can make a difference. About 85% of the children whose records were verified were already listed in health workers' registers, while 53% were subsequently vaccinated.However, migration, misinformation and vaccine hesitancy continue to pose challenges, making community outreach and regular follow-ups just as important as vaccine availability.The challenge does not end with just childhood immunisation.Limited awareness, high costs and poor access continue to hold back adult vaccination, particularly among senior citizens. Experts call for India-specific adult immunisation guidelines, with routine vaccination against influenza, pneumococcal disease, shingles and tetanus-diphtheria-pertussis, as well as hepatitis B shots for high-risk groups.Clearly, closing the vaccination gap will require more than free doses and digital records. Timely follow-ups, better awareness and easier access must go hand in hand to ensure people do not miss out on protection.The goal is to make vaccination a lifelong priority, not just a childhood routine.
Article Summary: India's vaccination story goes back more than two centuries. The first smallpox vaccination in the country was administered in Mumbai on June 14, 1802. Now, smallpox is history, polio has been eliminated, and maternal and neonatal tetanus are no longer public health threats in India.

Article Title: 'Malicious': India flays US court summons to NSA Doval, others over lawsuit by terrorist Pannun
Article Text:

NEW DELHI: The ministry of external affairs on Tuesday condemned "fabricated and malicious" attacks on New Delhi's officials after the US state department reportedly served the government with federal court summons in a civil case filed by designated terrorist Gurupatwant Singh Pannun.During the weekly press briefing, MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal termed the lawsuit as "frivolous", saying that requests for the service of judicial documents can only be routed through India's designated central authority."We reject the fabricated and malicious attacks on our high officials, as also the frivolous lawsuits," Jaiswal said."Requests for the service of judicial documents in India can only be routed through India's designated central authority, that is, the ministry of law and justice," he added.Last month, the US state department served federal court summons to New Delhi after Sikh separatist Pannun named number of Indian officials, including national security adviser (NSA) Ajit Doval and former chief of the Research and Analysis Wing (R&AW) Samant Goel.The order marks a fresh procedural development in the lawsuit, which concerns an alleged plot to assassinate Pannun in New York in 2023.The civil lawsuit is linked to the US department of justice's investigation into Nikhil Gupta, an Indian national described as a drug and arms smuggler.Gupta was arrested in the Czech Republic in 2023 before being extradited to the US.US prosecutors accused Gupta of conspiring with others to arrange the assassination of Pannun by hiring a hitman. According to the indictment, Gupta worked with Vikash Yadav, who was allegedly associated with the Research and Analysis Wing (RAW).In response to the allegations, the New Delhi set up a committee to investigate the concerns raised by Washington. Yadav, meanwhile, is facing a case in an Indian court.India has rejected Pannun's civil lawsuit, calling it "unwarranted and unsubstantiated".
Article Summary: The US state department reportedly served the government with federal court summons in a civil case filed by designated terrorist Gurupatwant Singh Pannun. MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal termed the lawsuit as "frivolous", saying that requests for the service of judicial documents can only be routed through India's designated central authority.

Article Title: 'Let us have a debate': Akhilesh Yadav challenges BJP over demonetisation
Article Text:

NEW DELHI: Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav on Wednesday renewed his criticism of the 2016 demonetisation exercise, calling it the "biggest corruption scandal in the world" and alleging that it had damaged banks, small traders and micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs).Addressing a press conference in Lucknow, Yadav invoked his "Khajanchi" jibe against demonetisation, marking 10 years of the child associated with his criticism of the currency ban.He said the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) should adopt Khajanchi and celebrate his birthday, while accusing the party of failing to acknowledge the consequences of the policy."Today Khajanchi turned 10. We have been celebrating its birthday since the beginning, but sadly the Bharatiya Janata Party has never celebrated Khajanchi's birthday. Bharatiya Janata Party should adopt it, but not how their MPs adopted villages," Yadav said.He alleged that demonetisation had increased cash circulation and described the exercise as "slow poison" for the economy. He also claimed that the move had been intended to "sink the banks".The SP chief questioned the government's banking reforms, including the merger and privatisation of banks, and alleged that demonetisation had weakened the banking system."The circulation of cash has increased by 70 per cent compared to what it was earlier. There is a long list of the damage that has been caused to MSMEs and small traders," he said.Yadav also criticised banks for deducting money from customers in the form of penalties, alleging that the banking system had become more difficult to navigate than dealing with moneylenders."Demonetisation became a curse for banks. Banks themselves were shut down, banks were merged, and even banks had to be sold," he said.He challenged the government to debate India's economic position at the time of Independence in 1947 and its stated ambition of becoming a developed country by 2047."The truth is that these people keep throwing around the slogan of a developed India by 2047. One negative decision like demonetisation has pushed India's economy even further behind the economic position we had in 1947, when we became independent," Yadav said."If they feel these allegations are not true, let us have a debate on this as well. Let there be a debate on what the economic situation was in 1947 and what it will be in 2047, and how far they have pushed us backwards," he added.The Centre announced the withdrawal of the old Rs 500 and Rs 1,000 currency notes on November 8, 2016, saying the move was aimed at tackling tax evasion and black money.The government has maintained that the exercise was successful in increasing the number of income tax returns filed.According to the finance ministry, the Income Tax Department conducted search and seizure operations against 900 groups between November 2016 and March 2017. These actions resulted in the seizure of Rs 900 crore, including cash worth Rs 636 crore, and the admission of undisclosed income of about Rs 7,961 crore.Opposition parties have repeatedly questioned whether demonetisation achieved its stated objectives.Yadav's remarks came amid a fresh exchange between the Samajwadi Party and the BJP in Uttar Pradesh. NEW DELHI: Nearly four out of five foreign medical graduates (FMGs) who appeared for the October 2026 Foreign Medical Graduate Examination (FMGE), mandatory for foreign-trained doctors seeking to practise in India, failed to qualify. Only 9,354 candidates passed, against 31,539 who failed, taking the pass percentage to 22.9%.The results come after months of protests by foreign medical graduates over the June examination, following which the National Board of Examinations in Medical Sciences (NBEMS) announced a series of measures based on an expert committee's recommendations. The October 31 examination was scheduled as an additional session to give candidates another opportunity to qualify.The committee had recommended a question-paper difficulty distribution of 30% easy, 50% moderate and 20% difficult questions. It also proposed allowing candidates to view their recorded responses, correct answers and marks awarded for individual questions.However, Dr Samar Kumar, National FMG In-charge, FAIMA, said feedback from candidates suggested that the October paper was moderate to difficult and did not appear to follow the recommended difficulty ratio.He said the October pass percentage of 22.86% was comparable to previous December-January sessions, while the June 2026 pass rate had fallen to around 12%. The absence of video-based questions in October may have contributed to the improvement, he said, as candidates had found them unfamiliar and time-consuming in June.Kumar also flagged the lack of clarity over the promised answer key, distant exam centres and late admit cards, which caused anxiety among candidates. He welcomed the fee reduction but urged NBEMS to clarify its commitments and ensure greater transparency.The results, declared by NBEMS on Tuesday, showed that of the 42,113 candidates listed, 1,190 were absent and the results of 30 candidates were withheld.An analysis of the score list showed that 14,613 candidates scored between 125 and 149 marks out of 300 but failed to meet the qualifying threshold of 150. Of these, 5,365 scored between 140 and 149, falling just short of the required marks.Candidates who qualify must undergo in-person identity and credential verification to receive their FMGE pass certificates. NBEMS said the reasons for withholding 30 candidates’ results had been communicated by email. Individual scorecards will be available from November 20 for six months, but cannot be used for registration with State Medical Councils in place of the pass certificate.NBEMS said subject experts reviewed all questions, awarding marks for technically incorrect questions and either accepted answer. Results remain provisional, and candidature may be cancelled if a candidate is found ineligible, even after the result or pass certificate is issued.

Article Title: Unesco: Women ahead in higher edu, but rural-urban gap hits schoolgirls

NEW DELHI: India has made substantial progress in closing the gender gap in education, with women now outpacing men in higher education. But a rural-urban divide continues to disadvantage girls at the school-completion stage. A Unesco report found that for every 100 boys completing upper secondary education in rural India, only 59 girls do so, compared with gender parity in urban areas. India has closed at least 65% of its initial disparity in upper secondary completion since 2000.The 2026 Global Education Monitoring report, Gender Equity in Access to Education, puts India's overall gender parity index for upper secondary completion at 0.89, or 89 girls for every 100 boys. In rural areas, it falls to 0.59.Unesco categorises India as having made "fast progress" among countries with large disadvantages for girls at the start of the century. This applies to students completing school within the expected age window and those finishing late.Recent govt data point to improvements in participation and retention. UDISE+ 2025-26 shows girls account for 48.4% of school enrolment. The secondary-stage dropout rate fell from 8.2% in 2024-25 to 7%, while retention rose from 47.2% to 51.9%.These indicators cannot be directly compared with Unesco's household-survey-based completion ratios.At college level, women lead men. AISHE 2023-24 puts the female gross enrolment ratio at 31.2%, against 28.9% for males. Women's enrolment rose from 1.57 crore in 2014-15 to 2.24 crore, a 42.2% increase. The higher education gender parity index stood at 1.08, with women's participation exceeding men's for seven consecutive years.Unesco's review of Indian studies found free school lunches had nearly twice the impact on primary enrolment for girls as for boys in disadvantaged rural communities. Separate toilets helped raise enrolment among adolescent girls, while girls' clubs offering life skills and social support modestly improved secondary completion in Karnataka Globally, Unesco found parity in enrolment from pre-primary through upper secondary school. Women increasingly outnumber men in higher education, with 88 male students for every 100 women enrolled and 82 male graduates. Yet 273 million children and young people were out of education in 2024.
Article Summary: Unesco: Women ahead in higher edu, but rural-urban gap hits schoolgirls. For every 100 boys completing upper secondary education in rural India, only 59 girls do so. India has closed at least 65% of its initial disparity in upper secondary completion since 2000.

Article Title: COP31 presidency pitches for global 35-by-35 electrification pledge, India may skip signing this informal commitment

NEW DELHI: The UN climate conference (COP31) presidency in Antalya, Turkiye, on Tuesday pitched for “35-by-35” global electrification pledge that aims to raise electricity’s share of the world’s final energy consumption from about 23 percent today to 35 percent by 2035, asking countries and businesses to join the initiative that will help the world in transitioning away from fossil fuels.Since the global electrification goal is a voluntary initiative of the COP31 presidency as a key headline issue of the current conference, many countries, including India, may not formally join this move being taken outside the formal negotiation process, even as most of them welcomed it in principle.India, which has already taken a big leap towards renewable energy and is gradually moving towards increasing its clean energy footprint, is expected to flag that the voluntary initiatives under the Presidency Action Agenda should remain separate from negotiations and that uniform global targets must respect national circumstances. In India, electricity currently makes up roughly 22 percent of the country’s total final energy consumption, with the remainder dominated by oil, coal and natural gas.The COP31 global electrification pledge, designed to usher in the “age of electricity”, will be achieved through electrifying transport, buildings and industry and will support global efforts to enhance energy security, expand energy access and reduce costs and emissions.The “35-by-35” target is based on the International Energy Agency (IEA) and International Renewable Energy Agency’s (IRENA) analysis of what is needed to keep the world on a pathway consistent with limiting warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels.“The COP31 Presidency is determined to chart a path forward and use the annual UN summit to build momentum. We are bringing everyone together to support each other and build collective momentum. The age of electricity is taking shape – and COP31 will be remembered as the moment we flicked the switch,” said COP31 President Murat Kurum while making the pitch for the “35-by-35” target.India, meanwhile, reaffirmed its commitment to climate multilateralism and the principles of equity and Common But Differentiated Responsibilities and Respective Capabilities (CBDR-RC), calling for a fair, equitable and ambitious outcome at COP31.Delivering India’s opening statement at COP31, Union environment secretary Narendra Bhooshan reiterated the country’s commitment to “contributing its fair share to global climate action while pursuing the development and well-being of its people”.On the critical issue of climate finance, he emphasised that public finance from developed countries remains central to catalysing climate action in developing countries and strengthening adaptation finance flows to address their vulnerabilities.

India’s sharp decline in extreme poverty has given the government much to celebrate. Prime Minister Narendra Modi hailed the World Bank’s latest findings as “A historic fall in poverty. A generational rise in opportunity.” He has linked the reduction in poverty to economic growth, infrastructure investment, welfare schemes and employment opportunities.The improvements are tangible. In 2011–12, roughly 27 out of every 100 Indians lived below the international extreme-poverty line of $3 a day. By 2023–24, fewer than three did. That is one of the fastest declines in poverty anywhere in the world. Yet the numbers reveal another, less discussed reality. About 57% of India’s poor live in a contiguous belt stretching from Uttar Pradesh to West Bengal, according to the World Bank’s October 2026 Poverty & Equity Brief.Globally, progress against extreme poverty has largely stalled . An estimated 81.1 crore people, or one in ten worldwide, live below $3 a day in 2026, virtually the same share as in 2019. Nearly 370 crore people, almost half the world’s population, live below the higher $8.30-a-day line.Slower growth, conflict and too few productive jobs have made further progress difficult.By comparison, India has made rapid progress. But the poverty that remains is concentrated in particular regions, and among households with fewer assets, less education and little access to stable, well-paying work. Further progress will increasingly depend on whether the states where poverty is concentrated can create better jobs and opportunities.Extreme poverty, measured at $3 per person per day, fell from 27.1% in 2011–12 to 2.6% in 2023–24. At the higher $4.20-a-day line, which the World Bank uses for lower-middle-income countries such as India, poverty fell from 57.7% to 16.1%. The Bank estimates that the number of people below this line dropped by 49.6 crore over the period. Both lines are international consumption benchmarks, set in 2021 purchasing-power-parity (PPP) dollars, which adjust for what money buys in each country.In 2023–24, about 3.7 crore Indians were below the extreme-poverty line. About 23.3 crore were living below $4.20 a day. That leaves roughly 19.6 crore Indians above the extreme-poverty threshold but still below the higher line.Jharkhand had the highest extreme-poverty rate among Indian states in 2023–24, at about 12.9%, according to the World Bank’s September 2026 Subnational Poverty and Inequality Database. Bihar’s rate was much lower, at 4.1%.In absolute numbers, however, the two states are almost level. TOI combined the World Bank’s state poverty rates with Health Ministry population projections. By that estimate, Bihar had about 51.8 lakh people below the $3 line, and Jharkhand 51 lakh.Uttar Pradesh provides another example. Its extreme-poverty rate was about 2%, but its population is so large that nearly 47 lakh people were still estimated to be below the line. At the higher $4.20 line, Jharkhand’s poverty rate was 41.2%, compared with 21.6% in Bihar, 20.1% in Uttar Pradesh and 14.5% in West Bengal.Yet Uttar Pradesh, at less than half Jharkhand’s rate, had the largest number of people below this line among the four states, about 4.73 crore. Bihar had another 2.74 crore, Jharkhand 1.63 crore and West Bengal 1.44 crore.Together, these four states were home to about 10.54 crore people below $4.20 a day, by TOI’s calculations. That is nearly 47% of the total when the estimates for every state and Union territory are added up. But large numbers of poor people are not confined to the northern and eastern belt.Maharashtra, one of India’s largest state economies, had an estimated 2.34 crore people below $4.20 a day, the third-highest state total after Uttar Pradesh and Bihar. Its poverty rate at this threshold was 18.5%, lower than those of Bihar and Jharkhand, but its large population pushed the absolute number much higher. Even at the $3 extreme-poverty line, Maharashtra had an estimated 40 lakh people below the threshold, the fourth-largest number among states.India’s own data on multidimensional poverty point the same way. NITI Aayog ’s National Multidimensional Poverty Index measures deprivation across health, education and living standards rather than spending alone.Its survey-based findings show that Bihar’s multidimensional poverty rate fell from 51.9% in 2015–16 to 33.8% in 2019–21. Jharkhand’s declined from 42.1% to 28.8%, and Uttar Pradesh’s from 37.7% to 22.9%. Even after these falls, about one in three people in Bihar was still poor on this measure at the time of the survey.In 2023–24, average monthly spending per person in rural Jharkhand was ₹2,946, against a national rural average of ₹4,122, according to the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation’s household consumption survey. That is about 29% lower than the national rural average. The same survey found that people in Jharkhand’s towns and cities spent 83% more on average than those in its villages, the widest urban-rural gap among India’s 18 major states.Employment has been a big driver of India’s fall in poverty. The World Bank estimates that the number of employed people rose by about 13.4 crore between 2017 and 2023, much of it driven by rural women entering work. An extra earner in a household can increase what the family spends and help it move above the poverty line. But the Bank notes that earnings, adjusted for inflation, stayed broadly unchanged, and much of the new employment was in relatively low-productivity work.According to the Periodic Labour Force Survey Annual Report 2025, 56.2% of employed Indians were self-employed, while 23.6% had regular wage or salaried jobs. Agriculture still accounted for 43% of employment. The share of regular salaried workers did rise, from 22.4% in 2024 to 23.6%, while agriculture’s share of employment fell.The government’s 2023–24 consumption survey found that average monthly spending per person was ₹3,652 in rural households dependent on casual farm labour, compared with ₹5,005 in rural households relying on regular salaried jobs outside farming. These figures measure household spending, not individual wages, but they show how much living standards vary with the type of work.Leaving farming does not automatically raise incomes, as Bihar shows. Services make up 58.7% of Bihar’s economic output, measured as gross value added, even though the state’s income per person is relatively low, according to the Union government’s Economic Survey 2025–26. But the survey notes that much of this output comes from low-value activities. By contrast, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu and Telangana together account for nearly 40% of India’s services output, supported by activities such as information technology, finance and professional services.A worker who leaves the fields for small-scale trading or another low-paying service job has moved into services too. But that does not necessarily bring the jump in earnings that a move into a more productive industry would. These states need jobs that pay better and offer a way up.Household spending data also miss some consequences of deprivation, such as poor child nutrition. The latest National Family Health Survey, NFHS-6, conducted in 2023–24, shows that child nutrition has improved substantially across India. The share of children under five who are stunted, or too short for their age, fell nationally from 35.5% in 2019–21 to 29.3%.All four states at the centre of this analysis improved too. Stunting declined from 42.9% to 35.6% in Bihar, from 39.6% to 35% in Jharkhand, from 39.7% to 31.5% in Uttar Pradesh and from 33.8% to 22.4% in West Bengal.But a fall in stunting has not always come with a fall in the share of underweight children.In Jharkhand, the share of children under five who were underweight, or too light for their age, rose from 39.4% to 41.1%, even as stunting declined. In Uttar Pradesh, the underweight share also rose, from 32.1% to 34.5%. Bihar improved on both counts, with the underweight share falling from 41% to 35.7%. So did West Bengal, where it fell from 32.2% to 28.5%.So far, India’s progress against poverty has been driven by rising consumption, more people in work and expanded government assistance, including food subsidies. The people still below the line may be harder to reach. As poverty falls, those who remain poor are increasingly concentrated in households with fewer assets, less education, more dependants and little access to stable employment.A young person growing up in a poorer district may have better chances at an education than their parents had, but no guarantee of a well-paying job nearby. The World Bank expects poverty to keep falling, though more slowly. Its projections suggest that the share of Indians below $4.20 a day will fall from 14.2% in 2026 to 12.1% in 2028.Living standards have improved across most states, including those in the northern and eastern belt. It is less clear whether growth can create more productive jobs and higher earnings in the places where a large share of poor households still live. Better infrastructure, education and healthcare will help. But households also need to be able to turn those gains into reliable incomes. India has already shown that poverty can fall sharply in just over a decade.The next phase will depend not only on lifting those still in extreme poverty, but also on what happens to the 19.6 crore Indians between the two poverty lines, who are above the lowest threshold but have yet to achieve economic security.
Article Summary: In 2011–12, roughly 27 out of every 100 Indians lived below the international extreme-poverty line of $3 a day. By 2023–24, fewer than three did. Prime Minister Narendra Modi hailed the World Bank’s latest findings as “A historic fall in poverty. A generational rise in opportunity”

Article Title: 'Our ties enjoy bipartisan support': India's first reaction to US midterm results
Article Text:
For India, the midterm outcome presents both opportunities and uncertainties.

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

In its first reaction to the US midterm election results, the ministry of external affairs (MEA) on Tuesday chose to emphasise the bipartisan nature of relations between the two countries while steering clear of commenting on the political outcome.The response comes against the backdrop of a significant political setback for US president Donald Trump, whose Republican Party lost control of both chambers of Congress in the November 3 midterm elections.Democrats secured a sweeping victory, winning control of the House of Representatives and the Senate, in a result that is expected to constrain Trump's legislative agenda during the final two years of his presidency.Responding to a question on the midterm results, MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said the elections were an internal matter of the United States and declined to offer any specific assessment."It is an internal matter of the United States. I have no specific comment on them beyond underlining that India and the United States' relationship enjoys bipartisan support in the United States. We continue to work to further strengthen our comprehensive global strategic partnership that we share with the US," Jaiswal said.The MEA said New Delhi remained committed to strengthening its comprehensive global strategic partnership with Washington, signalling that it expects ties to remain a priority irrespective of which party gains political ground in the US Congress. For India, the outcome presents both opportunities and uncertainties.The two countries have witnessed considerable turbulence in their relationship under Trump's second presidency, with disagreements over trade tariffs, India's purchases of Russian oil, immigration restrictions and Washington's approach towards Pakistan emerging as major irritants.The Democratic takeover of Congress could provide New Delhi with additional avenues to engage with lawmakers who have traditionally supported stronger India-US cooperation. It could also increase scrutiny of the Trump administration's policies, including its approach to trade negotiations and foreign relations. However, a Democrat-controlled Congress does not necessarily translate into an immediate change in Washington's policy towards India.The US president retains considerable authority over foreign policy and trade negotiations, meaning Trump will continue to play a central role in determining the trajectory of bilateral relations. At the same time, congressional oversight could influence decisions involving defence cooperation, technology transfers, immigration and trade.
Article Summary: MEA says it expects ties to remain a priority irrespective of which party gains political ground in the US Congress. Democratic takeover of Congress could provide New Delhi with additional avenues to engage with lawmakers who have traditionally supported stronger India-US cooperation. Congressional oversight could influence decisions involving defence cooperation, technology transfers, immigration and trade.

Article Title: Digital arrest scams: SC seeks prevention plan from WhatsApp & others, sends notice to RBI
Article Text:
Supreme Court seeks mandatory compensation for digital fraud victims if banks fail due diligence

SC wants banks to compensate digital fraud victims

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

SC seeks details of authorised financial institutions from RBI

NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court has asked WhatsApp and other digital intermediaries to submit details of the measures they propose to take to prevent digital arrest scams and related cybercrimes, directing them to share their proposals with the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre (I4C) as well.A bench headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, also comprising Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana, issued the direction in an order uploaded on the court's website following a hearing on October 29.The matter has been listed for further hearing on November 23.The case, taken up suo motu, is titled ‘In Re: Victims of Digital Arrest Related to Forged Documents’.“WhatsApp LLC (A Meta company) and other concerned intermediaries are also directed to apprise this Court of the measures they propose to undertake to prevent the digital arrest scams and related cybercrimes. They shall also simultaneously submit their proposals to the I4C,” the bench said.The court also reiterated its concerns over the role of financial institutions in preventing digital fraud, saying banks must be held accountable where their failure to exercise due diligence contributes to such crimes.In its October 29 order, the bench said the Reserve Bank of India 's proposed regulatory measures must include provisions requiring financial institutions to compensate victims when an investigation establishes that fraud occurred due to their failure to prevent or report suspicious activity.“We reiterate and emphasize that the regulatory measures proposed by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) must mandate and incorporate suitable provisions that require financial institutions to indemnify victims of digital arrest scams and other cyber frauds and pay suitable compensation not less than the amount lost by the customer,” the bench said.To ensure effective implementation of the proposed safeguards, the bench directed the RBI to submit a list of all authorised financial institutions before the next hearing.The court observed that although cybercrimes had declined by 50%, victims had still lost around Rs 800 crore so far this year.It said the RBI's proposed regulatory framework must include enforceable provisions for compensation, preventive intervention and institutional accountability.Describing banks as a “protective umbrella” for vulnerable customers, CJI Surya Kant said financial institutions had access to account holders' transaction histories and should use that information to identify and prevent fraudulent transfers before money leaves their accounts.
Article Summary: The Supreme Court has asked WhatsApp and other digital intermediaries to submit details of the measures they propose to take to prevent digital arrest scams and related cybercrimes. A bench headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant issued the direction in an order uploaded on the court's website following a hearing on October 29.

Article Title: ‘No order required’: Delhi HC on Central Secretariat Club’s plea against de-recognition after Centre rules out fresh allotment
Article Text:
HC refuses to halt Delhi’s entry curbs on non-BS-VI vehicles.

What's the case

NEW DELHI: The Delhi high court on Tuesday said no order was required on a petition challenging the directive to vacate the Central Secretariat Club after the Centre informed the court that it had no plans to allot the premises to anyone at present.The central government made the submission during an earlier hearing of a petition seeking an interim stay on its decision to de-recognise the club, formerly known as Talkatora Club.Taking note of the submission, the court ruled no order was required to be passed."Considering the above, no order is required to be passed. The petitioners are permitted to take away their belongings in the next one week. List on the date already fixed, that is, December 21, 2026," PTI quoted Justice Amit Mahajan as saying.The high court was hearing an application filed by the Central Secretariat Club seeking an ad interim stay on the July 14 de-recognition order and the July 17 eviction order.During the hearing on November 5, the Centre’s counsel submitted that there was no proposal to allot the premises to any party at this stage.The court had earlier issued notice to the central government and sought its response to the petition.The bench of Justice Mahajan was hearing the club’s challenge to the government’s de-recognition order and the eviction notice issued by the estate officer, directing it to vacate its premises in the President’s Estate.In its petition, the club alleged that the Department of Personnel and Training, through its July 14 order, had "arbitrarily, illegally and unconstitutionally" withdrawn the recognition granted to it.The petitioner contended that instead of acting on its complaints about alleged irregularities during the tenure of the ad hoc committee managing its affairs, the authorities withdrew its recognition in February without issuing a show-cause notice.Following the high court’s intervention, the club was granted a hearing, after which a fresh de-recognition order was issued on July 14.The petition described the July 14 de-recognition order and the July 17 eviction order as "ex facie arbitrary, malicious, unconstitutional, and a brazen, colourable exercise of administrative power."It further alleged that the authorities were attempting to use their own "administrative failures" and the "misconduct" of the ad hoc committee to forcibly dispossess the club and shut down the institution, calling it a "violation" of Article 14 of the Constitution and the principles of natural justice.The plea also challenged the eviction order for treating the 107-year-old institution, which had been granted permanent occupancy, as an "unauthorised occupant" on the basis of what it termed an "illegal cancellation" of allotment.
Article Summary: The Delhi high court said no order was required on a petition challenging the directive to vacate the Central Secretariat Club. The Centre informed the court that it had no plans to allot the premises to anyone at present. The central government made the submission during an earlier hearing of a petition seeking an interim stay on its decision to de- recognize the club.

Article Title: Watch: Tamil Nadu CM Vijay launches one-gram gold ring scheme for newborns
Article Text:
Vijay presented 22-carat, one-gram gold rings to 25 newborns. (PTI)

Who is eligible for the gold ring?

Scheme draws on Tamil tradition

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Tamil Nadu chief minister C Joseph Vijay on Monday rolled out the state government’s one-gram gold ring scheme for newborns in Madurai. He also held some of the newborns and presented the rings to beneficiaries during the launch programme.Under the scheme, eligible babies born in government hospitals and government primary health centres will receive a 22-carat, one-gram gold ring.The initiative, named the Maternal Uncle Gold Ring Scheme (Thaaimaman Thanga Mothiram Thittam), has an annual allocation of Rs 755.83 crore.It is aimed at celebrating motherhood, promoting maternal and child health and encouraging institutional deliveries by increasing public confidence in government healthcare facilities.The scheme will cover babies born on or after June 22, 2026, to mothers who are permanent residents of Tamil Nadu and have delivered at government healthcare institutions.Mothers must be registered under the Pregnancy and Infant Cohort Monitoring and Evaluation (PICME) system and have a Reproductive and Child Health (RCH) ID. They will also have to provide an e-KYC-verified Aadhaar card along with one of the prescribed identity or residence documents.These include ration cards, voter identity cards, Labour Welfare Board identity cards, Department of Posts address cards and nativity certificates.The state government has already procured 1.28 lakh one-gram gold rings for the initial rollout. Each ring will have a unique serial number and will be packed in tamper-proof packaging.From Monday, babies born in government hospitals will receive the rings at the time of discharge, according to the state government.To clear the backlog of eligible babies born between June 22 and Monday, the government will distribute the rings through 107 hubs across Tamil Nadu.Distribution will begin at the rate of 100 babies per day at each hub. At designated centres, 25 beneficiaries will be accommodated in the morning and another 25 in the afternoon to avoid overcrowding, PTI reported.Village Health Nurses will distribute invitations informing beneficiaries of their allotted date and time. Beneficiaries have been asked to visit the designated centres only at the time mentioned in their invitations.The district administration has also made transportation arrangements for beneficiaries from their respective areas. Vijay had announced the scheme ahead of the April 23 Assembly election as a symbolic gift to newborns, drawing on the Tamil tradition of ‘Thaimaaman Seer’. The scheme has retrospective effect from June 22, Vijay’s birthday.A government order issued on June 23 described the initiative as a token celebrating the birth of a child, motherhood and the cultural tradition of ‘Thaimaaman’.According to ANI, Tamil Nadu minister Arun Raj explained the cultural significance of the initiative saying, "A maternal uncle is someone who is among the first to rush in when a child is born, sharing in his sister’s happiness as his own. He assures her that he will always stand by her and her child, offering love, support and a sense of security.""Today, the Tamil Nadu Government, under the leadership of our brother, Mr. Vijay, is embracing this sacred bond of the maternal uncle and, as a gesture of that affection, is set to provide a one-gram gold ring to every child born in government hospitals. When the scheme was announced and the question arose as to where it should be launched, the place chosen by our Chief Minister was Madurai. This is the sacred soil of Madurai, blessed with the compassion and grace of Mother Meenakshi," he added.Tamil Nadu records around 7.8 lakh deliveries annually, with institutional deliveries accounting for 99.9% of births, according to NFHS-6. Government health facilities account for nearly 4.2 lakh deliveries, or around 53% of the total.According to the state government, the average out-of-pocket expenditure for a delivery at a government hospital is Rs 1,364, compared with Rs 63,473 at a private hospital.The government said the scheme is intended to encourage safe institutional deliveries, strengthen maternal and child welfare and increase public trust in government healthcare services.The Tamil Nadu Medical Services Corporation will procure the gold rings based on annual requirements, while a project and programme management unit will oversee implementation and monitoring.
Article Summary: Tamil Nadu chief minister C Joseph Vijay on Monday rolled out the state government’s one-gram gold ring scheme for newborns in Madurai. The scheme will cover babies born on or after June 22, 2026, to mothers who are permanent residents of Tamil Nadu and have delivered at government healthcare institutions. Vijay had announced the scheme ahead of the April 23 Assembly election.
